doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: What he thinks about when improvising
summary: He thinks melodically rather than by chords, relies on quick ears, and discusses risks of unfamiliar tunes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you’re improvising, are you thinking about the chords that are going by?

That’s a good question. I think it sort of depends on how well I know the song sometimes. When I’m improvising on a song that I’m familiar with, I’m not really thinking about the chords because they’re just sort of, I know them, I understand how the song is put together and how the chords fit together, and I’m thinking more about, really I guess the best answer is when you’re really improvising you’re not really thinking in a way. It’s more of like a Zen kind of thing really. It’s more like you just sort of, you’ve done your preparation, you know the song, and you’re just sort of in the moment, you know what I mean? You’re listening to what’s going on around you, and you’re thinking maybe about the melody or maybe you’re thinking about what the previous solo, what he ended with, you might just start with that idea and elaborate on that, or you’re basically just constructing a new melody. And I try to think more melodically than chordally in my solos, and just think of making a melodic line. But there’s times when I don’t know a song very well, which might very well happen here, where you’re really listening very hard to the chords and the bass, to hear how the harmony ties together. So you’re really listening to that and just trying to lock into that and then trying to jump to that other stage, like you know the song, without forgetting to listen to what’s going on around you. You might not know what’s coming ahead, and you have to really just react quickly. You have to have really quick ears and really quick reflexes sometimes, and just respond that way.
A very good description. And you hope that the bass player and the piano player know the tunes.

That could be a real problem. I’ve had those gigs where there’s the blind leading the blind and it can really be a disaster. But hopefully you have a leader who’s going to be smart enough to know what’s safe and what would make sense as far as songs that will come off. It doesn’t always happen. Of course we always take risks in jazz and that’s part of it. There’s a lot of times where at least somebody in the group doesn’t know the song as well as he’d like to, but like I said, you hopefully develop your ears enough so that you have these fast reflexes and you can respond to that.
I think there’s a certain amount of trying to make the audience think you know the song, even though maybe —
Yeah, I know the song, sure.
You never know. Sometimes the comments you get, people say, “Oh that was really, really great” and you’re feeling like whoa, I didn’t really know what I was doing there.

You’re wiping the sweat off like I guess I pulled that off, I don’t know. Yeah sometimes you feel like you might have been horrible because of the feelings going on inside you like you were just barely holding on, where if you’re a professional a lot of times you can play it off. And it happens.
